style="background:#DCDCDC;"|'''119,311''' |} ==Republican primary== The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] primary was hotly contested between [[Julianne Murray]], an attorney from [[Georgetown, Delaware|Georgetown]], and [[Colin Bonini]], a [[Delaware Senate|Delaware state senator]] from the [[Delaware's 16th Senate district|16th district]] and the Republican nominee for the [[governor of Delaware]] in [[2016 Delaware gubernatorial election|2016]]. Murray ended up winning the nomination. Although Bonini won Kent and New Castle counties, the latter of which is home to [[Wilmington, Delaware|Wilmington]] and is the most populous [[List of counties in Delaware|county in the state]], Murray won [[Sussex County, Delaware|Sussex County]], which is the most Republican county in the state and overall had the most votes, allowing her to carry the nomination. ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Julianne Murray]], attorney ====Eliminated in the primary==== * [[Colin Bonini]], state senator, nominee for Delaware State Treasurer in [[2010 Delaware elections#Treasurer|2010]], and nominee for [[List of governors of Delaware|Governor of Delaware]] in [[2016 Delaware gubernatorial election|2016]]{{Cite web|url=https://delawarestatenews.net/government/state-sen-bonini-running-for-governor-again/|title=State Sen. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Indiana|Governor]] | before_election = [[Eric Holcomb]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Eric Holcomb]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Indiana}} The '''2020 Indiana gubernatorial election''' was won by incumbent [[Republican Party (US)|Republican]] [[Eric Holcomb]] on November 3, 2020. The election was held concurrently with the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[2020 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[2020 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2020 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. [[Eric Holcomb|Holcomb]] was eligible to run for re-election to a second term in office, and announced his intention to do so on July 13, 2019, alongside his [[Lieutenant Governor of Indiana|lieutenant governor]], [[Suzanne Crouch]].{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Casey |title=Gov. Eric Holcomb to run for reelection: 'Let's keep making Hoosier history for four more years' |url=https://www.indystar.com/story/news/politics/elections/2019/07/13/gov-eric-holcomb-officially-announces-his-bid-re-election/1674492001/ |access-date=13 July 2019 |work=[[Indianapolis Star]] |date=July 13, 2019}} He faced [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Woody Myers]], the former health commissioner of Indiana (and later, of [[Commissioner of Health of the City of New York|New York City]]) and his running mate, [[Linda Lawson (politician)|Linda Lawson]], the former minority leader of the [[Indiana House of Representatives]], in addition to [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] Donald Rainwater, a [[U.S. Navy]] veteran and his running mate William Henry.{{Cite web|title=2020 General Election Candidate List - Abbreviated|url=https://www.in.gov/sos/elections/files/2020%20GE%20Candidate%20List%20-%2009.11.2020.pdf|website=Indiana Secretary of State (Election Division)|access-date=2020-10-02|archive-date=2020-10-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003235827/https://www.in.gov/sos/elections/files/2020%20GE%20Candidate%20List%20-%2009.11.2020.pdf|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=https://www.kokomotribune.com/news/local_news/libertarian-governor-candidate-donald-rainwater-to-visit-kokomo/article_9c72509e-1226-11eb-a73d-c7e8906f2232.html|title=Libertarian governor candidate Donald Rainwater to visit Kokomo|date=October 22, 2020|access-date=October 24, 2020|work=Kokomo Tribune}} Primary elections were held on June 2; Holcomb and Myers ran unopposed. In the general election, Holcomb won re-election to a second term. Myers also became the first major party candidate to receive fewer than one million votes since Republican [[David M. McIntosh|David McIntosh]] in [[2000 Indiana gubernatorial election|2000]].{{Cite web|url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?f=0&fips=18&off=5&elect=0&year=2000|title=2000 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Indiana|accessdate=31 March 2023}} The election was also notable for the strong performance of Libertarian candidate Rainwater, who finished in second place, behind Holcomb and ahead of Myers, in over one-third of Indiana's counties, 33 out of 92.{{cite news |last1=Martin |first1=Ryan |last2=Sikich |first2=Chris |title='We sent a message': Donald Rainwater doesn't win, sets Indiana Libertarian record |url=https://www.indystar.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/11/03/indiana-governor-election-libertarian-donald-rainwater-surge-results/6150140002/ |access-date=8 May 2021 |work=IndyStar}} The stronger-than-expected performance by Rainwater was perceived to be a reaction to Governor Holcomb's response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], with Rainwater pushing for fewer government restrictions.{{Cite web |last=Sikich |first=Chris |title=Indiana Libertarian candidate for governor targets voters upset by COVID-19 mandates |url=https://www.indystar.com/story/news/politics/2020/10/13/indiana-libertarian-candidate-governor-opposes-covid-19-measures/3624798001/ |access-date=2022-03-16 |website=The Indianapolis Star |language=en-US}} The Associated Press's large-scale pre-election survey found that Eric Holcomb won white Hoosiers 62–27%, while Myers won black Hoosiers 76–20%.{{cite news |title=Poll Results |url=https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2020/general-results/voter-analysis?race=G&state=IN|date=November 3, 2021}} This election marked the worst performance by a Democratic candidate for governor in Indiana history.{{Cite web |title=Our Campaigns - This is also one of the strongest performances for a third-party candidate in a statewide election in [[Indiana]], with [[Libertarian]] nominee Donald Rainwater receiving over 11% of the total vote. {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Montana|Governor]] | before_election = [[Steve Bullock (American politician)|Steve Bullock]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Greg Gianforte]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Montana}} The '''2020 Montana gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the next [[List of governors of Montana|governor of Montana]], concurrently with the [[2020 United States presidential election|U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[2020 United States Senate elections|elections to the U.S. Senate]] and [[2020 United States House of Representatives elections|the House of Representatives]] and various [[2020 United States elections|state and local elections]]. It resulted in voters selecting [[Greg Gianforte]] over [[Mike Cooney]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Steve Bullock (American politician)|Steve Bullock]] was term-limited and could not seek a third consecutive term in office, and he ran unsuccessfully for [[2020 United States Senate election in Montana|Montana's Class II Senate seat]].{{cite web |last1=Arkin |first1=James |title=Bullock enters Montana Senate race |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/03/09/bullock-enters-montana-senate-race-124260 |website=POLITICO |language=en |date=March 9, 2020}} Bullock's lieutenant governor, [[Mike Cooney]], was the Democratic nominee, while the Republican nominee was Montana's at-large representative [[Greg Gianforte]], who won the election, making him the first Republican governor of Montana since [[Judy Martz]] left office in 2005.{{cite web |last1=Gstalter |first1=Morgan |title=GOP Rep. Greg Gianforte wins Montana governor's race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/524417-gop-rep-greg-gianforte-wins-montana-governors-race |website=The Hill |language=en |date=January 18, 2021}} This was the only gubernatorial seat to change partisan control in the 2020 elections. This election marked the first time since the 1920s that Republicans controlled all state constitutional offices and a majority of the legislature.{{cite web |last1=Streep |first1=Abe |title=How Montana Took a Hard Right Turn Toward Christian Nationalism |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/11/magazine/montana-republicans-christian-nationalism.html |website=New York Times |language=en '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of North Carolina|Governor]] | before_election = [[Roy Cooper]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Roy Cooper]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in North Carolina sidebar}} The '''2020 North Carolina gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[governor of North Carolina]], concurrently with the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2020|elections]] to one-third of the [[United States Senate]] and elections to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[United States elections, 2020#State elections|state]] and local elections. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Roy Cooper]] was elected to a second term, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] lieutenant governor [[Dan Forest]]. Cooper became the first North Carolina governor to win re-election since [[Mike Easley]] in [[2004 North Carolina gubernatorial election|2004]]. He also outperformed other Democrats on the ballot and was the only Democrat to win a gubernatorial race in a state carried by [[Donald Trump]] in [[2020 United States presidential election|2020]]. With a margin of 4.51%, this election was the second closest of the [[2020 United States gubernatorial elections|2020 gubernatorial election cycle]] after [[2020 Puerto Rico gubernatorial election|Puerto Rico]] and the closest in a U.S. state. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Roy Cooper]], incumbent governor{{Cite tweet|number= 1202647745414205446 |user=RoyCooperNC|title=I've officially filed for re-election! '''Lenz:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996E2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674DE|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933E5|80–90%}} }} {{Elections in North Dakota}} The '''2020 North Dakota gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[Governor of North Dakota|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of North Dakota|lieutenant governor]] of North Dakota, concurrently with other [[2020 North Dakota elections|statewide elections]] and [[2020 United States elections|federal]] elections, including the [[2020 United States presidential election in North Dakota|U.S. presidential election]].{{cite web |title=North Dakota Election Laws |url=https://vip.sos.nd.gov/pdfs/Portals/2017%20to%202019%20Election%20Law%20Book.pdf |website=[[North Dakota Secretary of State]] |access-date=January 8, 2019}} Incumbent [[North Dakota Republican Party|Republican]] Governor [[Doug Burgum]] and Lieutenant Governor [[Brent Sanford]] were both re-elected to a second term. ==Republican primary== The [[North Dakota Republican Party|Republican Party]] held a state convention in the spring to endorse a single gubernatorial candidate. That candidate and his or her running mate were automatically placed on the primary election ballot. Endorsed candidates may or may not face competition from other candidates placed there by petition—as incumbent governor Burgum did in 2016. The winner of the primary appears on the general election ballot. All primary elections in North Dakota are open to all qualified North Dakota electors, regardless of party affiliation. The 2020 primary election was held on June 9. ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Doug Burgum]], incumbent governor{{cite web |last1=Dura |first1=Jack |title=Gov. {{legend0|#b3b3b3|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of New Hampshire|Governor]] | before_election = [[Chris Sununu]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Chris Sununu]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in New Hampshire}} The '''2020 New Hampshire gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[governor of New Hampshire]].{{Cite web |title=New Hampshire gubernatorial election, 2020 (September 8 Republican primary) |url=https://ballotpedia.org/New_Hampshire_gubernatorial_election,_2020_(September_8_Republican_primary) |access-date=2020-06-22 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en |archive-date=January 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220127030303/https://ballotpedia.org/New_Hampshire_gubernatorial_election,_2020_(September_8_Republican_primary) |url-status=live }} Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Chris Sununu]] was elected to a third two-year term in office with more than 65% of votes and winning every county, defeating his opponent [[Dan Feltes]], the Majority Leader of the Senate.{{cite web |url=https://www.unionleader.com/news/health/coronavirus/sununu-we-re-coming-out-of-winter-we-re-coming-out-of-covid/article_6841c05a-eb63-5ace-bf1f-b414bdcfc46c.html |title=Sununu: 'We're coming out of winter, we're coming out of COVID' |date=13 March 2021 |access-date=September 16, 2021 |archive-date=June 24, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624035506/https://www.unionleader.com/news/health/coronavirus/sununu-we-re-coming-out-of-winter-we-re-coming-out-of-covid/article_6841c05a-eb63-5ace-bf1f-b414bdcfc46c.html |url-status=live }} Nine governors ran for re-election in [[2020 United States gubernatorial elections|this cycle]] and all nine were re-elected. Sununu's win marked the first time since [[1986 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|1986]] that a Republican was elected to a third term as governor, in which year his father, [[John H. Sununu]] was reelected for his third and final term. The elder Sununu chose not to seek reelection in 1988, instead becoming [[George H. W. Bush]]'s chief of staff in 1989. Sununu became the first person to get more than 500,000 votes in the state's electoral history. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Utah|Governor]] | before_election = [[Gary Herbert]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Spencer Cox]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 69.17% {{increase}} }} {{Elections in Utah}} The '''2020 Utah gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[governor of Utah]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Gary Herbert]] declined to run for election to a third full term. == Background == Although incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Gary Herbert]] was eligible to run for re-election to a third full term, he initially announced shortly after being re-elected in 2016 that he would not run again, but indicated in January 2019 that he was open to the possibility of running again before ultimately deciding to retire and endorse his lieutenant governor, [[Spencer Cox (politician)|Spencer Cox]].{{cite news|last1=Gehrke|first1=Robert|title=Herbert wins his 3rd election as Utah governor|url=http://www.sltrib.com/home/4559987-155/herbert-appears-headed-to-victory-in|access-date=21 November 2016|publisher=The Salt Lake Tribune|date=8 November 2016}}{{cite news|url=https://www.deseretnews.com/article/900053102/utah-gov-gary-herbert-possible-re-election-bid.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130150112/https://www.deseretnews.com/article/900053102/utah-gov-gary-herbert-possible-re-election-bid.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 30, 2019|title=About face? Utah Gov. Gary Herbert says 'never say never' about possible re-election bid|last1=O'Donoghue|first1=Amy Joi|date=January 29, 2019|newspaper=Deseret News|access-date=January 30, 2019}}{{cite news |last1=O'Donoghue |first1=Amy Joi |title=Here are the reasons Utah Lt. Gov. Spencer Cox says he's running for governor in 2020 |url=https://www.deseretnews.com/article/900070594/spencer-cox-2020-utah-governor-race.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190515020317/https://www.deseretnews.com/article/900070594/spencer-cox-2020-utah-governor-race.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 15, 2019 |access-date=15 May 2019 |work=Deseret News |date=May 14, 2019}} Utah had not had a Democratic governor since [[Scott M. Matheson]] left office in January 1985. This is the second longest active streak of one-party leadership, trailing only [[South Dakota]], which had not had a Democratic governor since [[Harvey L. Wollman]] left office in 1979.{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Benjamin |title=Zachary Moses, a Democratic candidate for governor, wants to break up Republican control of Utah and build a space port |url=https://www.sltrib.com/news/politics/2019/07/19/zachary-moses-democratic/ |access-date=29 August 2019 |work=Salt Lake Tribune |date=July 19, 2019}}{{cite news |last1=Scott |first1=Dylan |title=Kristi Noem elected first woman governor of South Dakota |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2018/11/7/18055928/midterm-election-results-south-dakota-governor-kristi-noem-winner |access-date=August 26, 2019 |work=Vox |date=November 7, 2018}} The primaries took place on June 30, 2020. The filing deadline was on June 19, 2020. == Description == The 2020 Utah gubernatorial election was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[governor of Utah]], concurrently with the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2020|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] and elections to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[United States elections, 2020#State elections|state]] and local elections. The winner of the election was the first non-incumbent gubernatorial candidate to be elected since [[Jon Huntsman Jr.]] in 2004, who ran in this election before he was eliminated in the primaries. Lieutenant Governor Spencer Cox won the general election by defeating the Democratic nominee, [[University of Utah]] law professor and former [[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau|CFPB]] official [[Christopher Peterson (law professor)|Christopher Peterson]]. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Vermont|Governor]] | before_election = [[Phil Scott]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Scott]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 73.27%{{Cite web |title=Voter turnout |url=https://sos.vermont.gov/media/zgslplnf/voterturnout-4.pdf |website=sos.vermont.gov |access-date=11 November 2020}} {{increase}} }} {{Elections in Vermont}} The '''2020 Vermont gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[governor of Vermont|governor of the U.S. state of Vermont]]. As [[Vermont]] does not impose term limits upon its governors, incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Phil Scott]] was eligible to run for re-election to a third two-year term in office. On November 18, 2019, he confirmed that he was running for reelection, but did not yet publicly announce his campaign.{{cite news|title=Scott says he's undecided on 2020 — but he's already fundraising|url=https://vtdigger.org/2019/11/18/scott-says-hes-undecided-on-2020-but-hes-already-fundraising/|last=Landen|first=Xander|publisher=Vermont Digger|access-date=December 4, 2019}} On May 28, 2020, he officially announced his candidacy but stated that he would not campaign, maintain a campaign staff, or fundraise because of the state of emergency due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Vermont]]. The primary was held on August 11. Scott won re-election to a third term in a [[landslide victory|landslide]], defeating [[Vermont Progressive Party|Progressive]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee, [[Lieutenant Governor of Vermont|Lieutenant Governor]] [[David Zuckerman (politician)|David Zuckerman]]. Scott's 41-point victory margin was the largest in a Vermont gubernatorial election since [[1996 Vermont gubernatorial election|1996]] and the largest for a Republican candidate since [[1950 Vermont gubernatorial election|1950]], even while Democrat [[Joe Biden]] carried the state by a more than the 35-point margin in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Vermont|concurrent presidential election]], which was his strongest performance in the nation. Scott would improve upon his performance again in [[2022 Vermont gubernatorial election|2022]] and [[2024 Vermont gubernatorial election|2024.]] ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Phil Scott]], incumbent [[governor of Vermont]]{{Cite web|title=Gov. 2020 Washington gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2020 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2019}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2020 Washington gubernatorial election | country = Washington | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2016 Washington gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2016 | next_election = 2024 Washington gubernatorial election | next_year = 2024 | election_date = November 3, 2020 | image1 = File:Jay Inslee August 2019.jpg | image_size = 150x150px | candidate1 = '''[[Jay Inslee]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''2,294,243''' | percentage1 = '''56.56%''' | image2 = File:Loren Culp.png | candidate2 = Loren Culp | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 1,749,066 | percentage2 = 43.12% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2020 Washington gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|275px]] |County results |[[File:2020 Washington gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|275px]] |Congressional district results|[[File:2020 Washington gubernatorial election results map by precinct.svg|275px]] |Precinct results}} | map_caption = '''Inslee:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996E2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674DE|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0D0596|>90%}}
'''Culp:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}}
'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Washington|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jay Inslee]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jay Inslee]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Washington State}} The '''2020 Washington gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020. It followed a [[Nonpartisan blanket primary|top-two primary]] held on August 4. Incumbent Governor [[Jay Inslee]], the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] candidate, defeated Loren Culp, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] candidate by a wide margin. Inslee, who was eligible to run for a third term due to the lack of gubernatorial [[term limit]]s,{{cite news |last=Merica |first=Dan |title=Washington Gov. Jay Inslee announces 2020 presidential bid |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/03/01/politics/inslee-2020-presidential-campaign/index.html |date=March 1, 2019 |access-date=March 1, 2019}} initially [[Jay Inslee 2020 presidential campaign|launched a campaign]] for [[president of the United States]] in [[2020 United States presidential election|the 2020 election]]. When he dropped out of that race in August 2019 due to extremely low polling numbers,{{Cite web|date=2019-10-21|title=Was Jay Inslee's presidential campaign a failure?|url=https://theaggie.org/2019/10/21/was-jay-inslees-presidential-campaign-a-failure/|access-date=2020-10-20|website=The Aggie|language=en-US}} he announced he would seek a third term as governor.{{cite news |author=Dan Merica and Paul LeBlanc |title=Washington Gov. Jay Inslee drops out of presidential race |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2019/08/21/politics/jay-inslee-drops-out-of-race/index.html |access-date=August 22, 2019 |work=CNN |date=August 22, 2019}} Several other Democratic political figures considered entering the race if Inslee did not run, including [[Washington Attorney General]] [[Bob Ferguson (politician)|Bob Ferguson]]; no other major Democratic candidates entered the race.{{cite news |last=Gutman |first=David |date=August 22, 2019 |title=With Inslee running again for governor, leading Washington state Democrats put their ambitions on hold |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/politics/with-inslee-running-again-for-governor-leading-washington-state-democrats-put-their-ambitions-on-hold/ |work=The Seattle Times |access-date=August 22, 2019}} Republican Loren Culp, the [[police chief]] of [[Republic, Washington]], placed second in the top-two primary and advanced to the general election alongside Inslee. The election was clear and decisive, with Inslee winning re-election over Culp by over 13 points. This marked the largest margin of victory in a Washington gubernatorial race since [[Gary Locke]] won reelection in [[2000 Washington gubernatorial election|2000]]. Inslee's landslide victory included him winning over 74% of the vote in [[King County, Washington|King County]], the highest for a Democratic gubernatorial candidate in the county's history. King County, home to [[Seattle]], has about a third of the state's voters.{{cite news|last=Brunner|first=Jim|date=November 10, 2020|title=Republican Loren Culp lost King County by the worst margin in at least four decades in Washington governor's race|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/politics/republicans-face-political-chasm-in-king-county-as-democrats-lose-some-rural-support/|work=[[The Seattle Times]]|access-date=November 21, 2020}}{{cite news|url=https://www.sos.wa.gov/elections/research/election-results-and-voters-pamphlets.aspx|title=Election Results and Voters' Pamphlets|work=Washington Secretary of State|access-date=November 21, 2020}} In addition, Inslee became the first Democratic gubernatorial candidate since the aforementioned Locke in 2000 to win any county in [[Eastern Washington]], namely [[Whitman County, Washington|Whitman County]], home to [[Washington State University]].{{cite news|last=Leadingham|first=Scott|date=November 19, 2020|title=Incumbent's Advantage: Why Whitman County Votes For Biden And Inslee, But GOP For Congress|url=https://www.nwpb.org/2020/11/19/incumbents-advantage-why-whitman-county-votes-for-biden-and-inslee-but-gop-for-congress/|work=Northwest Public Broadcasting|access-date=December 12, 2020}} Culp still ran ahead of the top-ticket presidential candidate, [[Donald Trump]], by about four points. Despite the margin of victory, Culp refused to concede and filed a lawsuit against Republican [[Secretary of State of Washington|Washington Secretary of State]] [[Kim Wyman]] five weeks after the election.{{cite web |title=Refusing to concede lost election, Washington gubernatorial candidate Loren Culp sues Sec. of State |url=https://www.seattlepi.com/local/politics/article/loren-culp-demands-audit-over-nov-election-results-15795563.php |publisher= Seattle Post-Intelligencer |access-date= December 19, 2020 |date= December 11, 2020|first= Callie|last= Craighead}} He did not give a [[Concession (politics)|concession speech]], while making claims of irregularities which Wyman characterized as "unsubstantiated".{{cite news|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/politics/loren-culp-refusing-to-concede-washington-gubernatorial-race-turns-on-top-republicans/|title=Loren Culp, refusing to concede Washington gubernatorial race, turns on top Republicans |date= November 21, 2020|first =Jim| last= Brunner|work = [[The Seattle Times]]}} Culp's actions drew criticism and were compared to [[Donald Trump]]'s refusal to concede the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]].{{cite web |last1=Bowman |first1=Nick |title=Opinion: Loren Culp, Trump show a refusal to accept reality in both Washingtons |url=https://mynorthwest.com/2300275/opinion-loren-culp-trump-rejection-reality-both-washington/ |website=MyNorthwest.com |publisher=Bonneville International |access-date=10 November 2020 |date=9 November 2020}} This election marked the tenth consecutive victory of the Democratic candidate for governor of Washington. ==Background== Washington had not had a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor since [[John Spellman]] left office in 1985, the longest streak of Democratic leadership of any state in the country and the third longest streak of one-party leadership after [[South Dakota]] (which had not had a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor since [[Harvey L. Wollman]] left office in 1979) and [[Utah]] (which had not had a Democratic governor since [[Scott M. Matheson]] left office nine days prior to Spellman in 1985).{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Benjamin |title=Zachary Moses, a Democratic candidate for governor, wants to break up Republican control of Utah and build a space port |url=https://www.sltrib.com/news/politics/2019/07/19/zachary-moses-democratic/ |access-date=August 29, 2019 |work=Salt Lake Tribune |date=July 19, 2019}}{{cite news |last1=Scott |first1=Dylan |title=Kristi Noem elected first woman governor of South Dakota |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2018/11/7/18055928/midterm-election-results-south-dakota-governor-kristi-noem-winner |access-date=August 26, 2019 |work=Vox |date=November 7, 2018}}{{cite news |last1=Camden |first1=Jim |title=John Spellman, Washington's last Republican governor, dies |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2018/jan/16/former-gov-spellman-dies/ |access-date=August 23, 2019 |publisher=The Spokesman-Review |date=January 16, 2018}} Incumbent Governor [[Jay Inslee]], who previously served in the [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]], was first elected to the governorship in [[2012 Washington gubernatorial election|the 2012 election]] and won reelection [[2016 Washington gubernatorial election|in 2016]]. When Inslee announced [[Jay Inslee 2020 presidential campaign|his candidacy]] for president, several political figures expressed interest in running for Governor if Inslee won [[2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries|the Democratic primaries]]. These included [[List of Attorneys General of Washington|Attorney General]] [[Bob Ferguson (politician)|Bob Ferguson]], [[Washington State Department of Natural Resources#Commissioner of Public Lands|Commissioner of Public Lands]] [[Hilary Franz]] and [[King County Executive]] [[Dow Constantine]].{{Cite web |url=https://www.king5.com/article/news/politics/king-county-executive-dow-constantine-not-ruling-out-run-for-governor/281-b1ecff63-ef9e-49ee-8fd6-992706c85b26 |title=King County Executive Dow Constantine not ruling out run for governor |date=February 22, 2019 |publisher=KING 5 News |access-date=February 25, 2019}} They stated they would only run if Inslee did not, avoiding a [[primary challenge]].{{cite news |last1=Axelrod |first1=Tal |title=Inslee to announce bid for third term as Washington governor: report |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/458382-inslee-to-announce-bid-for-third-term-as-washington-governor-report |website=The Hill |date=August 22, 2019 |access-date=August 22, 2019}} Several [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] politicians announced their own campaigns to challenge Inslee, including businessman Anton Sakharov, [[Republic, Washington|Republic]] police chief Loren Culp, and [[Washington State Senate|state senator]] [[Phil Fortunato]]. However, speculated candidates such as former U.S. Representative [[Dave Reichert]], former [[Port of Seattle|Seattle Port Commissioner]] and 2016 gubernatorial candidate [[Bill Bryant (politician)|Bill Bryant]], [[Pierce County Executive]] and former state senator [[Bruce Dammeier]], and state House Minority Leader [[J. T. Wilcox]], all declined to be candidates, leaving no prominent Republicans to challenge Inslee, which was seen as a necessary prerequisite to mount a formidable challenge to him. == Primary election == Washington is one of two states that holds a [[top-two primary]], meaning that all candidates are listed on the same ballot regardless of party affiliation, and the top two move on to the general election. '''Salango:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = [[Governor of West Virginia|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jim Justice]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jim Justice]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in West Virginia}} The '''2020 West Virginia gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2020, to elect the [[governor of West Virginia]], concurrently with the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[United States Senate elections, 2020|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], elections to the [[United States House of Representatives]] and various [[United States elections, 2020#State elections|state]] and local elections. Incumbent Governor [[Jim Justice]] announced his 2020 re-election campaign on January 7, 2019.{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=Haley |title=Governor Justice announces 2020 campaign |url=https://wvva.com/news/top-stories/2019/01/07/governor-justice-announces-2020-campaign/ |access-date=January 7, 2019 |publisher=WVVA |date=January 7, 2019 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Justice was elected in [[2016 West Virginia gubernatorial election|2016]] as a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]], but later switched back to the Republican Party at an August 2017 campaign rally with [[Donald Trump]].{{cite news|title=West Virginia Undergoing Political, Generational Change|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/03/us/politics/west-virginia-governor-to-switch-from-democrat-to-republican-trump.html|access-date=August 3, 2017|newspaper=New York Times|date=August 3, 2017}} Justice won re-election to a second term, defeating Democratic [[Kanawha County, West Virginia|Kanawha County]] commissioner Ben Salango. Justice's re-election made him the first Republican to be elected governor of West Virginia since [[Cecil Underwood]] in [[1996 West Virginia gubernatorial election|1996]]. Additionally, Justice became the first incumbent Republican governor to win re-election since [[Arch A. Moore Jr.]] in [[1972 West Virginia gubernatorial election|1972]], as well as the first Republican to carry all counties in West Virginia. However, Justice performed worse than Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, who outperformed Justice by 5.13 percentage points. Additionally, Salango slightly outperformed Biden by 0.53 percentage points.
